title: Introduction to DBMS
definition_text:
A Database Management System (DBMS) is software that allows users and applications to create, store, organize, retrieve, update and manage data in a database.

It acts as an interface between users and the database. When a user requests information, the DBMS processes that request, communicates with the database and returns the required result.

A DBMS also provides important facilities such as data security, access control, data integrity, backup and recovery, and transaction management. These facilities help ensure that data remains accurate, protected and available to authorized users.

Examples of DBMS software include MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle Database and SQLite.
example_text: Spotify uses a DBMS to link millions of tracks, playlists, and user listening histories.

title: History of DBMS
summary: Trace the evolution from 1960s Hierarchical and Network models to Codd’s Relational Model and modern Cloud/NoSQL systems.
definition_text: DBMS technology evolved from rigid 1960s Navigational databases (Hierarchical IMS & Network CODASYL) to Edgar F. Codd’s 1970 Relational Model (tables + SQL), followed by Object-Relational, NoSQL, and distributed cloud databases.
example_text: Before 1970, programmers wrote complex pointer-chasing code to walk tree paths. Codd’s Relational Model let anyone ask "what" they wanted with SQL instead of "how" to navigate pointers.

Codd paper + System R / SQL"],["1990s","Object-Relational","Complex types, multimedia & warehousing"],["2000s+","NoSQL & NewSQL","Web-scale JSON documents & distributed SQL"]]}

In the 1970s–80s, SQL and commercial RDBMSs (Oracle, DB2, Ingres) dominated. title: Applications of DBMS
summary: Discover how Banking, Airlines, E-Commerce, Healthcare, Universities, and Telecom rely on DBMS daily.
definition_text: DBMS powers almost every modern digital domain—including Banking & Finance (transfers, ledgers), Airlines (real-time seat reservations), Universities (courses & transcripts), E-Commerce (inventory & orders), Healthcare (EHRs), and Telecommunications (call & billing logs).
example_text: When you buy the last concert ticket online, the e-commerce DBMS locks that inventory row so nobody else can purchase the same ticket.

title: SQL ALTER TABLE
summary: Evolve existing table schemas safely with ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN, RENAME, and DROP COLUMN.
definition_text: ALTER TABLE: DDL statement modifying an existing table’s structure (add/rename/drop columns or constraints). `ALTER TABLE table_name ADD COLUMN new_col TYPE;` adds a column to an existing populated table. You can also `RENAME TO`, `RENAME COLUMN`, or `DROP COLUMN` as schemas evolve.
example_text: Adding `linkedin_url TEXT` to an existing `students` table in production. Example: PRAGMA table_info('students');

title: SQL Constraints Overview
summary: Enforce data quality automatically inside the database with column-level and table-level Constraints.
definition_text: SQL Constraints: Schema rules enforced by the DBMS to preserve entity, domain, and referential integrity. Constraints are rules enforced automatically by the DBMS on INSERT and UPDATE: `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`, `PRIMARY KEY`, `FOREIGN KEY`, `CHECK`, and `DEFAULT`. Rejecting bad data inside the database protects every app connecting to it.
example_text: Guaranteeing no student ever gets saved with a negative GPA or duplicate email. Example: PRAGMA table_info('enrollments');

Execution Outcome","role":"Shows NOT NULL and composite PRIMARY KEY flags on `enrollments`.","sample":"Constraints guarantee data integrity at the database layer regardless of which client writes data."}]}

title: SQL UNIQUE Constraint
summary: Prevent duplicate values in columns like email or course_code using UNIQUE.
definition_text: UNIQUE Constraint: Constraint ensuring all values in a column or column group are distinct across rows. The `UNIQUE` constraint ensures every non-NULL value in a column (or combination of columns) is distinct across all rows. Unlike `PRIMARY KEY`, a table can have MULTIPLE `UNIQUE` constraints (e.g., both `email` and `national_id`).
example_text: Enforcing unique `course_code` (`CS301`) and unique `email` in `students`. Example: SELECT student_id, email FROM students;

Execution Outcome","role":"Every student holds a distinct email guaranteed by a UNIQUE constraint.","sample":"UNIQUE prevents duplicate values and allows multiple unique columns per table."}]}
practical_explanation: Every student holds a distinct email guaranteed by a UNIQUE constraint.

title: SQL CHECK Constraint
summary: Restrict allowed column values to valid business rules using CHECK (condition).
definition_text: CHECK Constraint: Domain integrity rule verifying that column values satisfy a boolean expression. `CHECK (gpa >= 0.0 AND gpa <= 4.0)` verifies a boolean condition on every INSERT or UPDATE. If the condition evaluates to FALSE, the database rejects the write immediately.
example_text: `CHECK (salary > 0)` or `CHECK (credits BETWEEN 1 AND 6)`. Example: SELECT full_name, gpa FROM students WHERE gpa BETWEEN 0.0 AND 4.0;

Execution Outcome","role":"Verifies all student GPAs obey the valid [0.0, 4.0] domain.","sample":"CHECK validates custom value ranges and business rules on every row write."}]}

title: SQL AUTO INCREMENT
summary: Use engine-specific generated-key features while allowing for gaps in generated IDs.
definition_text: AUTO INCREMENT: Column attribute automatically generating sequential unique integers for new rows. Auto-incrementing keys automatically assign `1, 2, 3...` on each new INSERT: MySQL uses `AUTO_INCREMENT`, PostgreSQL uses `SERIAL` / `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`, SQL Server uses `IDENTITY(1,1)`, and SQLite uses `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT`.
example_text: Automatically assigning `order_id = 1001, 1002, 1003` as customers check out. Example: SELECT MAX(student_id) AS current_highest_id FROM students;
diagram_config_json: {"layers":[{"id":"u3_1","label":"1. SQL Construct","role":"AUTO INCREMENT","sample":"SELECT MAX(student_id) AS current_highest_id FROM students;"},{"id":"u3_2","label":"2. Execution Outcome","role":"The next auto-incremented insert automatically receives `highest_id + 1`.","sample":"AUTO INCREMENT / IDENTITY generates unique Primary Key numbers automatically on INSERT."}]}
practical_sql: SELECT MAX(student_id) AS current_highest_id FROM students;
practical_explanation: The next auto-incremented insert automatically receives `highest_id + 1`.
lesson_content_json: {"simpleIntro":"Nobody manually tracks \"What was the last student ID—482 or 483?\" AUTO INCREMENT generates unique IDs safely every time a row is inserted.","detailedExplanation":"Identity or auto-generated key features assign a value when an insert omits the key, but they do not promise gap-free sequences. title: Selection (σ) and Projection (π)
summary: Master unary operators Selection σ (horizontal row filter) and Projection π (vertical column filter).
definition_text: Selection (σ) & Projection (π): σ filters rows by condition; π picks columns and eliminates duplicate rows. Selection `σ_p(R)` keeps tuples in relation `R` that satisfy predicate `p` (equivalent to SQL `WHERE`). Projection `π_A1,A2(R)` extracts only columns `A1, A2` and automatically removes duplicate tuples because relations are sets (equivalent to `SELECT DISTINCT`).
example_text: `π_full_name(σ_dept_id="CS"(students))` finds names of all CS students. Example: SELECT DISTINCT full_name FROM students WHERE dept_id = 'CS';

Practical SQL Link","role":"Executes Selection (WHERE) followed by Projection (SELECT DISTINCT).","sample":"SELECT DISTINCT full_name FROM students WHERE dept_id = 'CS';"}]}

By discarding irrelevant tuples early, it cuts I/O, memory usage, and CPU time on large student tables.","Projection (π) removes unneeded columns, shrinking each tuple's width and thus the amount of data transmitted across network layers or stored temporarily. This column‑level pruning speeds up result rendering and lowers bandwidth consumption for client applications.","Because relational algebra treats relations as sets, projection automatically eliminates duplicate rows, providing a built‑in DISTINCT effect without extra syntax. title: Transaction Management
summary: Understand logical units of work, transaction states (Active, Committed, Aborted), and concurrency control.
definition_text: Database Transaction: Logical unit of work moving a database from one consistent state to another via COMMIT or ROLLBACK. A Transaction is a sequence of database reads/writes treated as a single indivisible unit of work (`BEGIN`, `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`). Its lifecycle moves from Active -> Partially Committed -> Committed (durable), or Failed -> Aborted (rolled back cleanly).
example_text: Booking a flight + charging a credit card inside one atomic transaction. Example: SELECT project_id, project_name, budget FROM projects;

practical_sql: SELECT project_id, project_name, budget FROM projects;
practical_explanation: Multi-project budget transfers require Transaction Management to keep totals balanced.

This atomicity protects data integrity across interdependent tables.","Transaction management provides concurrency control mechanisms such as locking and multiversion concurrency, allowing many users to read and write simultaneously without corrupting shared data. As a result, high‑throughput applications like enrollment systems maintain consistent state even under heavy load.","By writing changes to a write‑ahead log before they become visible, transaction management guarantees durability, so committed updates survive crashes or power failures. title: ACID Properties
summary: Master Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability—the four pillars of reliable database transactions.
definition_text: ACID Properties: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability—core guarantees of reliable DBMS transactions. ACID describes transaction properties: Atomicity treats a transaction as all-or-nothing; Consistency means a correctly formed transaction preserves declared invariants; Isolation controls how concurrent work is observed, with guarantees depending on the chosen isolation level; and Durability means committed changes survive failures according to the engine’s configuration and storage guarantees. Serializable isolation aims for an outcome equivalent to some serial order; weaker isolation levels allow more concurrency anomalies.
example_text: Even if power dies 1 millisecond after ATM confirmation, Durability guarantees the updated balance survives. Example: PRAGMA journal_mode;

This eliminates data anomalies and simplifies error handling.","Consistency enforces all defined constraints, triggers, and referential integrity rules before and after a transaction, ensuring that business invariants such as budget limits remain valid. title: Second Normal Form (2NF)
summary: Remove Partial Dependencies on composite keys so every non-key column depends on the WHOLE Primary Key.
definition_text: Second Normal Form (2NF): 1NF relation where no non-prime attribute depends on only part of a composite candidate key. A relation is in Second Normal Form (2NF) if it is in 1NF and no non-prime attribute is partially dependent on any candidate key. This means every non-prime attribute must depend on the whole candidate key, not a proper subset. If all candidate keys are single-attribute, 2NF follows from 1NF; having a single-column primary key alone does not rule out a composite alternate candidate key.
example_text: Removing `course_title` from `Enrollments(student_id, course_id, course_title, grade)` into `Courses(course_id, course_title)`. Example: SELECT e.student_id, c.course_code, c.title, e.grade FROM enrollments e JOIN courses c ON e.course_id = c.course_id LIMIT 5;
